1:
Matthew Henry gives the praise three purposes and denies it is flattery. It is meant to encourage her under her dejections, since whatever others thought she was amiable in his eyes; to teach her what to value herself upon, not external advantages but the comeliness of grace put upon her; and to invite others to think well of her too. All the beauty of the saints, he adds, is derived from him, so that they shine by reflecting his light; the repetition marks both the certainty of the thing and the pleasure he takes in saying it. John Wesley adds a caution about method: since the beauty is described part by part, we need not labour to fit each particular to a distinct grace, the design of the whole being to show the completeness the church has in part received and will more fully receive.

The word rendered locks is the chapter’s first crux. Charles Ellicott says the derivation and cognate Arabic words leave no doubt that it means veil, and calls the rendering given here, out of thy silence, strange and meaningless — a defect the Latin mystified further into from that which lies hid within, a fruitful source, he says, of moral allusion to the hidden beauties of the soul. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result by grammar, refusing the reading that makes it hair flowing down like a mane, since the preposition cannot be used of the eyes in relation to braids hanging before them; the verb means to stop up or wrap oneself about, so the veil is named as what closely hides the face. Adam Clarke supplies the object: a partial veil of black goat’s hair hung from the crown by silken cords, leaving forehead and eyes bare while covering the rest of the face; one such, lately brought from Egypt, lay before him as he wrote.

The flock on the mountain is as contested. Ellicott reports contradictory interpretations of the verb, the Latin giving which have ascended and the bulk of commentators the exact opposite, come down or hang down; only the context can decide, and any rendering suggesting dark hair flowing round the shoulders is allowable. He adds that the long, soft, black hair of the eastern goat is probably meant as much as the look of the whole flock on the hillside. Wesley keeps to the facts of the place: the hair of goats there was of extraordinary length and softness, and the country was hilly and wooded and fit for breeding them.

On the teeth the voices divide. John Gill reports an old physician’s observation that human teeth resemble a sheep’s in figure and order, and holds the whiteness chiefly intended; the Targum applies them to the priests, but he prefers the ministers of the Gospel, teeth being firm and sharp to prepare food. Ellicott presses the Hebrew, which means to make double and may mean to occur in pairs as well as to bear twins, the second giving far better sense: the rows are exactly paired, upper to lower, like sheep coming two and two from the washing. Wesley says the same more briefly, that the twins denote the two rows and that not one tooth is lacking.

Two more corrections close the passage. Keil and Delitzsch identify the scarlet as the worm-colour, the red juice of the cochineal, and argue that the word rendered speech is properly the mouth, named as the organ by which the soul expresses itself, the poet wanting a fuller word than the plain one. Ellicott agrees from the parallelism and corrects temples to cheeks behind the veil, quoting a Persian ode in which the pomegranate recalls the blushes of the beloved. Clarke takes the figure from the cut side of the fruit, where the blush is finest, though the inside may be meant, streaked with red and white.
4:
The tower is easier to describe than to find. Charles Ellicott doubts it can be identified, since even two towers minutely described by the ancient historian cannot be located, and the structure known since the Crusades by that name is far later; the Greek version treats the disputed word as a proper name, rabbinical authority makes it a model for architects, and most modern commentators, differing over the etymology, still reach the sense our version gives. Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the tower of the flock, from which the king surveyed his people, and note that elsewhere it is called the tower lying out from the royal house, a building on Zion used as a court of justice. John Gill allows either the stronghold of Zion or a tower built as an armoury, and derives the word for armoury from a root meaning to teach, refusing the readings that make it a pattern for craftsmen or a lighthouse, and taking it for the place where learners of the art of war laid up their weapons.

Gill insists on what the comparison is not: the neck is likened to a tower not for height, an outstretched neck being a token of pride, but for being hung with spoils as a neck is hung with pearls and chains. Adam Clarke offers a modern parallel, the pillars seen in armouries with weapons arranged on them in many shapes, such as anyone who has visited the armoury in the tower of London will have seen.

On the next comparison they diverge in method. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the figure, the pair compared for equality and youthful freshness and the bosom to a meadow of lilies; and they observe that the praise stops here, counting seven things named, the eyes, hair, teeth, mouth, temples, neck and breasts, a sevenfold beauty. Clarke refuses the game altogether: he has met many attempts to justify the similitude and judges them unworthy of citation, holding that the poet speaks the language of nature, that language often fails an impassioned lover so that his comparisons come out without strict correctness, and that the description shows more nature than art.

Who speaks the sixth verse decides its reading. Keil and Delitzsch give it to the bride and say that all who continue it as the king’s words lose themselves in absurdities, since they must make the mountain of myrrh and hill of frankincense stand for her attractions, and the figures would be grotesque. Wesley notices that the same words were spoken by the bride earlier and are returned here by the bridegroom in answer, understanding the hill of the church on earth, where believers are directed to look for Christ. Gill agrees that they are Christ’s words, and reads the daybreak as the day of grace rising on an elect sinner and the shadows as ignorance and unbelief in flight. Clarke keeps the day literal, the morning breeze and the setting sun, and places the mountain among hills where myrrh and incense trees grew; Ellicott renders it until the day breathe, that is, when evening is come, and holds that the hills only carry the previous figure forward, the curtain falling on the end of another day.

Keil and Delitzsch take the modesty of her reply as what makes her lovelier still, and read the absence of blemish as covering soul and body alike, since the earlier verses praised her outward beauty while the sixth let her soul appear. Gill turns it into doctrine, a completeness in Christ as to justification and, in sanctification, a perfection of parts though not of degrees, belonging to the weakest member as much as the strongest. Clarke glosses it as every part of thee is beautiful, thou hast not a single defect, and sets beside it a Latin poet’s catalogue of a nymph’s beauties, ending by believing the beauties yet unseen the best.
8:
The new title is noticed by all. John Gill observes that spouse appears here for the first time, the day of espousals being now past, and that it is used chiefly to press her to come. Matthew Henry counts the occurrences, twice spouse and three times sister and spouse, and takes the change of address as marking a covenant: she is called his spouse only after the day of espousals, and his calling her so makes her so. Since no single human relation is sufficient, Henry adds, he owns her under two that among men are incompatible, for a man who said of his wife that she was his sister was understood to be denying she was his wife, whereas the church is both to Christ at once. Charles Ellicott treats the word soberly: the same Hebrew is rendered daughter-in-law, bride or spouse according as the relation is viewed from the parents’ side or the husband’s, and its use here does not by itself prove a completed marriage, since sister is joined to it next verse and it may be only a stronger endearment. Adam Clarke thinks the word peculiar and reports the suggestion that a Jewish princess is meant, the title sister marking one of the same stock and so distinguishing her from an Egyptian bride — the ground of a theory that two queens appear in the song, which he calls probable while declining to contend for any system.

The call itself turns on two vowel points. Ellicott prefers to me over with me, noting that the Greek and Latin read simply hither, a difference only in the pointing, and that the word rendered look has in the Greek its primitive sense of come. He reads the whole verse as another reminiscence of the obstacles that had attended the union, the rocks and snows that shut in the poet’s northern home and the beasts that haunted them standing for difficulty, so that, like a modern poet’s shepherd who holds that love is of the valleys, he calls her down from inaccessible heights; to suppose a literal journey to these peaks one after another he calls absurd, since they are named as emblems of height.

Keil and Delitzsch reject a rival construction on three grounds. On that reading the king announces that instead of lonely mountains and dangerous caves she shall inhabit the palace with him; but the Hebrew would have to be built differently to say it, she does not come from that range at all, and such an answer would not meet her longing for quiet.

Clarke takes the picture as fiction. He reports a commentator who sees an admirable poetic invention here, the beloved represented as a mountain nymph occupied in hunting the lion and the leopard, a bold and undisciplined girl unwilling to leave her wild retreats, whom the king invites down with the promise of a crown; the classical poets, Clarke adds, described their huntress goddess in just those terms. John Wesley uses the same wildness as an argument rather than a picture, since the places where she was are not only barren but dangerous, being inhabited by lions and leopards, and the height is what allows her to see the place she is invited to.

Gill declines the literal mountain altogether. It is not the range north of the land, famous for its fragrant trees, that is meant, but the temple built of its timber and the city that held it, which in Christ’s time had become a den of thieves and out of which he called his people; or else, the mountain being a pleasant one, it stands for the carnal pleasures from which he calls them off. He also notes a rendering that turns the invitation into a promise, thou shalt come with me, the coming being the effect of a powerful grace and a drawing love rather than of persuasion.
9:
The verb of the ninth verse pulls two ways. Charles Ellicott reports that many give it the exactly opposite sense to our version, thou hast emboldened me, and grants that the literal thou hast hearted me will bear either, the language of love approving equally stolen my heart and given me thine; but the mention of the neck-chain settles it, the poet saying playfully that his heart was caught by that chain. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result by asking what is fitting: the form can mean to make courageous, but it would be strange for a man who is no coward, and a king at that, to say that his love gives him heart, however well it might suit a warrior daring the uttermost for a woman’s admiration. Adam Clarke glosses it bluntly as thou hast hearted me, taken away my heart, as one says a man has barked a tree or fleeced a flock.

Clarke also defends the single eye, thought harsh and much emended; the margin’s at once has twenty manuscripts behind it, but he judges the change unnecessary, since one glance says enough and the poet may be describing a look given in passing, when only one eye could be seen. He takes the chain for the play of the muscles of the neck rather than a necklace. John Wesley makes the doubling the point: the love cannot be sufficiently expressed by any one relation.

On the next verses the praise moves to what she says and how she smells. Keil and Delitzsch note that the two words praise her love first as it strikes the eye and then as it is known on nearer acquaintance, and that praise of her person is mixed with praise of her fragrance, since her soul speaks not only by her lips but breathes out of her spices; the praise, they add, is sensuous, but carries a moral consecration. Clarke supplies the classical parallel, that eloquence was compared to honey and milk by the ancients, as in the epic where words sweeter than honey flow from the old counsellor’s tongue; the figure, he says, is common to all writers and languages. John Gill applies it to the church’s speech in prayer, praise, ministry and common conversation, pressing the manner of it, that the words drop freely and without constraint, at proper seasons, and continually. Wesley reads the ointments as the gifts and graces of the Spirit.

The garden is where they most nearly agree. Ellicott says the closed garden and sealed fountain appear to have been established metaphors for the pure and chaste wife, and cites a prayer still used at Jewish marriages, that no stranger may enter the sealed fountain. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by way of Greek custom and poetry: among the Athenians the women’s apartment was not only locked but sealed, and a tragedian praises a wife who had not broken her seal of conjugal faith. Having established the plain sense, Clarke ends by exclaiming how many will make metaphors out of metaphors.

Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fill in details. Gill reports two candidates, a rocky valley below certain pools which the friars point out, and, more probably, the king’s garden near the city, shut up and kept for the king’s own use; the church answers to it in being marked off from the world’s wide waste, and in its fruitfulness. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the words, one term for the water denoting the bubbling wave and the other the place, as it were an eye of the earth, from which the spring gushes; a reformer distinguished the two rightly, they note, while all the old translators rendered as though the same word stood in both places. Wesley keeps it practical: the enclosure is the care of providence, the shutting up a preservation from pollution, as springs were shut where water was scarce.
13:
What the plants stand for divides them. Adam Clarke takes them for the fecundity of the bride, and says the remaining expressions refer wholly to matters of a connubial nature. Charles Ellicott reports that some have thought the offspring of the marriage meant, but holds that the poet is plainly describing the charms of his beloved in the language of flowers, and adds that the pomegranate may have been an emblem of love, held sacred to a goddess. Keil and Delitzsch take the list as a figure for every utterance of her personality, and quote a commentator who wished he knew how to unlock it, since in the flower-language of love all these fruits must have had their interpretation; in old German poetry, they note, to break flowers meant to enjoy love. Both they and John Gill take the word for orchard to be an old Persian one for an enclosed park, though Gill reports a derivation from a root meaning to separate, and Clarke notes that paradise comes from it.

Ellicott turns botanist: the saffron is a bulb whose dried pistil and stigma make the spice; the calamus he leaves open, there being many sweet grasses in the East; the cinnamon probably covers two species, the rind being what is used, the plant belonging to the laurels and growing in Ceylon and on the Malabar coast.

Who speaks the fifteenth verse changes its force. Gill and Matthew Henry both give it to the church, Gill reading the phrases in the vocative, so that she calls him the fountain of gardens and the well of living waters, and Henry making it her acknowledgment that she owes him all the glory of her fruitfulness — those who are gardens to Christ must acknowledge him a fountain to them. John Wesley takes it the other way and keeps her the fountain, since being shut up does not mean she keeps her waters to herself, the church conveying to believers the life she receives. Keil and Delitzsch mark what has changed: the earlier comparison turned on the collecting and sealing up, this one on the inner life and its outward activity, a well of living water being one in which what it gives out springs up from within, so that it is at once received and its own.

The winds are the last dispute. Clarke reports that the south wind there is extremely hot in summer, and passes on a proposal that the verb we render come means rather enter thy repositories, so that the line should read arise, thou north wind, and retire, thou south, the beloved being invited into his garden by the coolness of the air rather than shut indoors by the heat. Gill raises two objections to the plain reading, that the verb blow is singular and construed only with the south, and that opposite winds cannot blow together; he reports the view that the north wind is told to depart, it being spring. Keil and Delitzsch notice which wind is missing, the east being left out because the idea of what is destructive attaches to it.

On the meaning the allegorists agree. Henry makes the Spirit the wind, a north wind of conviction and a south wind of comfort, graces in the soul answering to the spices, and notes that we can invite Christ to nothing but what is already his own. Ellicott stays with the poem, hearing the airs of love called to blow so that the perfumes may flow out and the beloved no longer keep herself reserved; he compares a modern poet on woodbine spices wafted abroad when a breeze of morning moves, and holds that the last clause should stand as a separate verse, the maiden’s answer, in which she yields. Clarke ends by complaining that commentators take a literal sense where the metaphor is plain and then build an allegory on a metaphor.
